summary: JSON Web Signature (JWS) represents content secured with digital signatures or Message Authentication Codes using JSON-based data structures. The cryptographic algorithms it uses are described in the separate JSON Web Algorithms specification.

eli5.summary: A JWS is a note with a signature on it so you can tell who wrote it and that nobody changed it.

questions: what is a json web signature
what is the difference between jws compact and json serialization
what does the alg header parameter do in jws
subtitle: A JSON-based way to sign or MAC any content so recipients can check it was not changed.

tldr.problem: Applications that already use JSON need a standard, compact way to protect an arbitrary sequence of octets against modification, using either digital signatures or Message Authentication Codes (MACs).
tldr.mechanism: A JWS combines a JOSE header, a payload and a signature, each base64url encoded. It has a compact dot-separated form and a JSON form that can carry several signatures.
tldr.outcome: Recipients can verify integrity, and with signatures the origin, of content in a URL-safe string or a JSON object. Algorithms are defined separately in the JWA specification.

facts.label: Compact form
facts.value: 3 base64url parts separated by exactly 2 periods

today: RFC 7515 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its algorithms are defined in RFC 7518, and RFC 7519 builds the JSON Web Token on top of it.

sections.title: What a JWS Is
sections.content:
JSON Web Signature (JWS) represents content secured with digital signatures or Message Authentication Codes (MACs) using JSON-based data structures. The mechanisms give integrity protection for an arbitrary sequence of octets.

Two serializations are defined. The JWS Compact Serialization is a compact, URL-safe form meant for space-constrained places such as HTTP Authorization headers and URI query parameters. The JWS JSON Serialization is a JSON object that allows multiple signatures or MACs on the same content. Both share the same cryptographic basis.

Algorithms and identifiers live in the separate JSON Web Algorithms (JWA) specification, and encryption is covered by JSON Web Encryption (JWE). Names are kept short because a core goal is compact output.
sections.eli5: A JWS puts a tamper-proof seal on a message. You can pick a small seal that fits on one line or a bigger form that lets several people sign.

sections.title: Parts of a JWS
sections.content:
A JWS has three logical values: the JOSE Header, the JWS Payload and the JWS Signature. The payload is the octets being secured and can be anything, not only JSON. The signature is a digital signature or MAC over the protected header and the payload.

The JOSE Header is made of Header Parameters. Those split into the JWS Protected Header, which is integrity protected by the signature, and the JWS Unprotected Header, which is not and can appear only in the JSON Serialization. In the compact form the entire JOSE Header is the protected header.

What gets signed is the JWS Signing Input: ASCII(BASE64URL(UTF8(JWS Protected Header)) || '.' || BASE64URL(JWS Payload)). Base64url here means base64 with the URL-safe alphabet of RFC 4648 and all trailing = characters omitted. An Unsecured JWS has no integrity protection and uses the alg value none.
sections.eli5: A signed note has a label on top, the message in the middle and the stamp at the bottom. The stamp is made from the label and the message together, so changing either one ruins it.

sections.title: Compact and JSON Serializations
sections.content:
The Compact Serialization is three base64url values joined by periods: protected header, payload, signature. Exactly two periods separate them. It supports only one signature or MAC and has no syntax for an unprotected header.

The JSON Serialization is neither optimized for compactness nor URL-safe. Its general syntax has a payload member and a signatures array. Each array element holds protected, header (the unprotected header, as a plain JSON object) and signature. At least one of protected and header must be present per signature so that alg is conveyed. The two header sets MUST have disjoint parameter names.

The flattened syntax is for a single signature. It drops signatures and moves protected, header and signature to the top level beside payload. Applications must say which serialization features they use, and implementations need only support what their applications need.
sections.eli5: The short version is one line with three chunks separated by dots. The long version is a form with labelled boxes, and it can have several signature boxes.

sections.title: The JOSE Header Parameters
sections.content:
Header Parameter names MUST be unique. A parser must either reject duplicates or use a JSON parser that returns only the lexically last one, as ECMAScript 5.1 specifies. Parameters not understood MUST be ignored, unless they are listed in crit.

Registered parameters include alg, the algorithm used, which MUST be present and understood. Others are the key hints jku, jwk, kid, x5u, x5c, x5t and x5t#S256. There are also typ and cty, which declare media types for the whole JWS and the payload, and crit.

The crit parameter lists extension parameters that recipients MUST understand, or else the JWS is invalid. It MUST occur only in the protected header and MUST NOT be an empty list. New parameter names should be registered with IANA or use a collision-resistant name, and should be introduced sparingly because they can make JWSs non-interoperable.
sections.eli5: The header is the label that says how the note was stamped and which key to use. Some labels are optional hints, but one, the stamp type, is always required.

sections.title: Creating and Validating a JWS
sections.content:
To create a JWS, make the payload and header, base64url-encode them, compute the signature over the signing input, base64url-encode that, and output the serialization. For the JSON Serialization, repeat the header and signature steps for each signature or MAC.

To validate, parse the parts, base64url-decode the protected header and verify it is valid UTF-8 JSON, build the JOSE Header and check for duplicate names, and check that all required fields are understood. Then decode the payload and signature and verify the signature over the signing input using the algorithm named in alg.

With multiple signatures, at least one MUST validate or the JWS MUST be considered invalid. Which others must validate is an application decision. A valid signature is not enough: the application SHOULD treat the JWS as invalid if the algorithm is not acceptable to it. String comparisons follow the JSON rules of RFC 7159, except for typ and cty values.
sections.eli5: Making a signed note means writing it, labelling it and stamping it. Checking one means undoing each step and seeing whether the stamp still fits.

sections.title: Finding the Right Key
sections.content:
The recipient must be able to determine which key was used. This can be done with the header parameters jku, jwk, kid, x5u, x5c, x5t and x5t#S256, or by means outside the specification. The producer SHOULD include enough information to identify the key unless the application has another convention.

These parameters MUST be integrity protected if they are used in a trust decision. If the only thing the decision uses is the key itself, protection is not needed, because swapping in a different key makes validation fail. A kid is only a hint, and its structure is unspecified.

Where a URL is used (jku or x5u), an HTTP GET MUST use TLS and the server identity MUST be validated. How shared symmetric keys are exchanged is outside the scope of this RFC.
sections.eli5: To check a stamp you need the right stamp-checker. The note can carry hints about which one to use, but how people share secret stamps is not covered here.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Keys are only as strong as their entropy: a minimum of 128 bits should be used for all keys. Signer private keys and MAC keys must be protected, and the key distribution method must authenticate the origin of keys.

MACs and signatures differ. A MAC key is held by every party that uses it, so validating a MAC only shows the message came from one of those parties, and it cannot prove origin to a third party.

Implementations MUST check that the algorithm encoded inside a signature matches alg. To resist algorithm substitution, carry alg in the protected header, which is always the case in the Compact Serialization. Also avoid timing differences between successful and failed operations, and use a unique message identifier in the protected content to resist replay.

JSON validation must be strict. Malformed JSON, or valid JSON followed by extra characters, MUST cause the JWS to be rejected. Names must be compared verbatim after escape processing, so sig equals \u0073ig but SIG does not.

An Unsecured JWS uses alg of none and has an empty signature. It provides no integrity protection at all.
sections.eli5: A stamp is only as good as the secrecy and quality of the stamp-maker. A tricky person might try to swap stamp types, so checkers must be strict about every detail.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC creates the IANA registry of JSON Web Signature and Encryption Header Parameters, where new names are added on a Specification Required basis after a three-week review by Designated Experts. It recommends that registered names not exceed 8 characters without a compelling reason. The initial entries are the parameters from the header section.

It also registers two media types: application/jose for a JWS or JWE in Compact Serialization, and application/jose+json for the JSON Serialization.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of label names so that nobody invents two labels with the same name meaning different things.
